case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the objective knowledge standard from Safeco Insurance Co. v. Burr applies to the False Claims Act's scienter requirement, or whether a defendant's subjective intent controls when determining liability for fraudulent claims involving ambiguous legal obligations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: False Claims Act (FCA), 31 U.S.C. § 3729 et seq., specifically the 'knowingly' scienter requirement, in conjunction with the interpretive framework established by Safeco Insurance Co. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (relators Schutte, Yarberry, and Proctor), supported by the United States, Senator Grassley, 33 states, and the National Whistleblower Center, argue that the FCA's scienter requirement is fundamentally subjective in nature, meaning that a defendant's actual subjective intent and knowledge at the time of submitting claims should govern liability. They contend that the Seventh Circuit's application of Safeco's objective reasonableness standard improperly shields defendants who subjectively knew their claims were false but can retroactively construct an objectively reasonable legal interpretation, thereby gutting the FCA's anti-fraud enforcement mechanism and undermining the government's primary tool for combating fraud in federal contracts and programs.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents SuperValu Inc. and Safeway Inc. argue that the objective knowledge standard articulated in Safeco v. Burr should control FCA scienter analysis when a claim's falsity turns on an ambiguous legal obligation. They assert that all seven courts of appeals to address the question have uniformly adopted this standard, creating strong persuasive consensus, and that defendants who act under an objectively reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous legal requirement — absent authoritative guidance to the contrary — cannot be said to have 'knowingly' submitted false claims, thereby protecting good-faith actors from ruinous FCA liability.
key_precedents: Safeco Insurance Co. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) — established the objective reasonableness standard under the Fair Credit Reporting Act's 'willfully' requirement, which lower courts extended to the FCA
False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 et seq. — the primary federal statute at issue defining 'knowingly' to include actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard

Seventh Circuit decisions in United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu Inc. (No. 21-1326) and United States ex rel. Proctor v. Safeway Inc. (No. 22-111) — the consolidated lower court rulings under review
Decisions from all seven circuits that had previously addressed the Safeco-FCA question, uniformly applying the objective standard prior to this Supreme Court review

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference is remarkably unified, and I find Justice Barrett's textualist analysis particularly well-constructed: Congress's self-contained definitional work in § 3729(b)(1) leaves no gap for courts to fill by importing Safeco's objective gloss from a materially different statutory scheme. My minimalist instincts counsel me to consider whether there is a narrower ground — for instance, holding only that Safeco does not categorically preclude FCA liability when subjective bad faith is demonstrated, without fully resolving whether Safeco has any role in FCA cases — but the textual case against Safeco's wholesale importation is strong enough that a broader holding may be warranted. The strongest counterargument for respondents is that an objective safe harbor provides fair notice and prevents overcriminalization of regulatory ambiguity, but Justice Kagan correctly identifies that Congress already addressed this concern by requiring subjective scienter rather than strict liability, and defendants who genuinely and subjectively believed their claims were lawful will not satisfy the reckless disregard standard. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward a holding that is textually grounded but leaves open whether Safeco's framework might inform the outer boundaries of 'reckless disregard' in truly ambiguous cases, preserving some doctrinal flexibility without undermining the core subjective inquiry Congress mandated.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively and persuasively reinforced what the statutory text makes plain: Congress in 1986 enacted a self-contained, tripartite definition of 'knowingly' that is inherently subjective in character, leaving no textual gap for courts to fill with Safeco's objective reasonableness gloss. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies the absurdity that would result from the Seventh Circuit's approach — it would render the FCA's scienter standard narrower than a simple 'specific intent to defraud' requirement, which Congress expressly disclaimed, producing a result no faithful reading of the statute can sustain. Justice Barrett's point about the incompatibility of Safeco's objective framework with the FCA's self-contained definition is particularly well-taken from an originalist and textualist standpoint: when Congress provides its own precise definition of a mental state term, courts have no license to override that definition by borrowing from judicial constructs developed under materially different statutory language. The strongest argument for respondents — that Safeco provides a workable, settled framework that courts have applied for years — fails under my methodology because longevity of judicial error does not transform that error into fidelity to the statutory text Congress actually enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett have both correctly identified the core textual problem with the Seventh Circuit's approach: Congress in 1986 enacted a self-contained, three-pronged definition of 'knowingly' that is inherently subjective, and importing Safeco's objective reasonableness gloss from the FCRA's materially distinct 'willfully' language would require us to override an unambiguous congressional definition with a judicial construct borrowed from an inapposite statute. The strongest argument for the respondents — that Safeco provides a workable, administrable standard that prevents overdeterrence of legitimate conduct — fails on its own terms in the FCA context because the common-law backdrop for fraud statutes, unlike the FCRA's consumer protection context, has always centered on subjective intent, as Halo Electronics confirms. I would add to my colleagues' reasoning that the practical consequences here are particularly troubling: sophisticated healthcare contractors like SuperValu, with contemporaneous internal evidence of subjective doubt about their compliance, should not be able to escape liability merely by retaining counsel to construct a post-hoc objectively reasonable interpretation, as that result would effectively immunize the most culpable actors — those who knew they were pushing the boundaries — while only catching the most reckless. The Court should hold that the FCA's scienter inquiry is governed by the statute's own text, asking what the defendant actually knew, deliberately ignored, or recklessly disregarded at the time of submission.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Kagan's observation that the Senate Report accompanying the 1986 amendments confirms Congress was deliberately expanding liability to reach defendants who subjectively knew or should have known their claims were problematic — the precise opposite of what an objective safe harbor would accomplish. Justice Thomas's textualist point also resonates with my own analysis: the three-pronged definition of 'knowingly' in § 3729(b)(1) is self-contained and exhaustive, leaving no gap for courts to fill by importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard from the materially distinct FCRA context. From my pragmatic perspective, the real-world consequences of the Seventh Circuit's approach are devastating — corporations like SuperValu and Safeway can retroactively construct plausible legal interpretations to shield conduct that was subjectively fraudulent, leaving Medicaid beneficiaries and taxpayers without meaningful recourse. The strongest argument for respondents — that Safeco provides a workable, fair standard that protects good-faith actors — fails because the FCA already protects genuinely good-faith actors through its subjective framework: a defendant who truly believed its claims were accurate has no actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard to speak of, making the objective safe harbor unnecessary except as a shield for bad-faith actors.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's point about the 'deliberate ignorance' and 'reckless disregard' prongs being effectively read out of the statute by Safeco's objective standard is particularly compelling and reinforces my own textual analysis — if an objectively reasonable legal interpretation can shield a defendant who subjectively knew their claims were problematic, Congress's tripartite definition becomes a nullity in precisely the cases it was designed to reach. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies the absurdity problem: a Safeco-derived objective safe harbor would render the FCA's scienter provision *narrower* than a simple 'specific intent to defraud' requirement, which Congress expressly rejected in the 1986 amendments. The strongest counterargument from the respondents' position — that Safeco provides fair notice and prevents overdeterrence of legitimate conduct — fails on its own terms in the FCA context, because the statute's deliberate ignorance prong already incorporates a limiting principle: defendants who genuinely and in good faith investigated their compliance obligations and reached reasonable conclusions will not have 'consciously avoided' knowledge of falsity. The textual architecture is self-sufficient and needs no Safeco supplement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett's observation that importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard would effectively read the 'deliberate ignorance' and 'reckless disregard' prongs out of the statute entirely is particularly compelling from a textualist standpoint — Congress enumerated three distinct mental states precisely because it wanted each to do independent work, and an objective safe harbor would collapse all three into a single inquiry about post-hoc legal plausibility. The strongest argument for Respondents would be that Safeco provides a workable limiting principle preventing FCA liability from sweeping in genuinely good-faith actors who relied on ambiguous regulatory guidance, but this concern is adequately addressed by the statute's own text: a defendant who genuinely and subjectively believed its interpretation was correct lacks 'actual knowledge,' 'deliberate ignorance,' or 'reckless disregard' of falsity, so no Safeco overlay is needed. The Seventh Circuit's error was conflating the question of what standard governs with the evidentiary question of how a defendant proves subjective good faith — the latter is a trial question, not a reason to graft an objective test onto an unambiguous statutory definition. As Justice Kagan notes, the 1986 legislative history confirms Congress was deliberately expanding liability beyond narrow actual-knowledge standards, making the Seventh Circuit's approach a direct inversion of congressional purpose.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan's point about the Senate Report confirming Congress's deliberate expansion of liability to reach subjective bad faith reinforces my own textual analysis: the 1986 amendments were a considered legislative response to courts that had been too permissive toward defendants, and the Seventh Circuit's Safeco transplant resurrects exactly the evasion Congress sought to foreclose. The strongest argument for respondents would be that Safeco reflects a general common-law principle about scienter in ambiguous regulatory contexts that transcends the FCRA's specific text — but as Justice Alito correctly notes, Halo Electronics already rejected that move in the patent context, demonstrating that Safeco's objective framework is tethered to its specific statutory home and cannot travel freely. From an institutionalist standpoint, I am also mindful that allowing courts to override Congress's explicit definitional work with judicially imported standards from inapposite statutes would undermine the Court's credibility as a faithful interpreter of legislative text rather than a policy-making body. The unanimity of my colleagues across very different methodological commitments — from Justice Thomas's strict textualism to Justice Sotomayor's purposivism — itself signals that the statutory text here is genuinely unambiguous in its subjective orientation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's observation that applying Safeco's objective standard would render the FCA's scienter provision *narrower* than if Congress had simply written 'specific intent to defraud' is particularly compelling — it exposes the Seventh Circuit's approach as producing an absurd result that no faithful textual reading can sustain. The strongest argument for Respondents would be that Safeco represents a general common-law principle about scienter in ambiguous regulatory contexts that courts should apply absent contrary congressional direction, but that argument fails here precisely because Congress *did* provide contrary direction: the 1986 definition of 'knowingly' in § 3729(b)(1) is a self-contained, carefully enumerated statutory definition that displaces any need to resort to common-law gap-filling from an inapposite statute. Justice Alito's citation of Halo Electronics v. Pulse Electronics further reinforces that this Court has already declined to extend Safeco's framework when the underlying statutory text and common-law backdrop differ — and the FCA's fraud-law backdrop is categorically distinct from the FCRA's consumer-protection context. The unanimity of my colleagues' reasoning across methodological perspectives — from textualism to purposivism — reflects that the statutory text here is genuinely unambiguous, and I see no argument from the Respondents' side that would require me to reconsider.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Kagan's observation that the 1986 Senate Report confirms Congress was deliberately expanding liability to reach defendants who subjectively knew or should have known their claims were problematic — the precise opposite of what an objective safe harbor would accomplish. Justice Barrett's textualist point is equally compelling: the FCA's definition is self-contained and self-sufficient, and importing Safeco's objective gloss from the FCRA's materially distinct 'willfully' language would override Congress's own definitional work with a judicial construct drawn from an inapposite statutory scheme. The strongest argument for respondents would be that Safeco provides a workable, administrable standard that prevents FCA liability from chilling legitimate regulatory ambiguity, but that concern is adequately addressed by the FCA's existing scienter framework — defendants who genuinely and subjectively believed their interpretations were correct will not satisfy the actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard prongs. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that allowing sophisticated corporate defendants to retroactively construct objectively reasonable legal interpretations as a scienter shield creates precisely the kind of asymmetric procedural advantage that insulates powerful actors from accountability while leaving Medicaid beneficiaries and the public without meaningful recourse.

John Roberts.reasoning: The statutory text of 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) is dispositive here: Congress explicitly defined 'knowingly' to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard, while expressly rejecting any specific intent requirement. This carefully crafted, three-pronged definition reflects a deliberate congressional choice to focus on a defendant's subjective state of mind at the time of submission, not a post-hoc objective reasonableness inquiry. Safeco was decided under the FCRA's 'willfully' requirement — a materially different statutory term with different common-law roots — and importing its objective framework into the FCA context would require this Court to override an unambiguous congressional definition, which my commitment to statutory text and institutional restraint counsels strongly against. The narrow, minimalist path here is simply to apply what Congress wrote: if a defendant subjectively knew, deliberately ignored, or recklessly disregarded the falsity of a claim, the FCA's scienter requirement is satisfied regardless of whether a lawyer can later construct an objectively reasonable interpretation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A) is unambiguous: Congress in 1986 deliberately defined 'knowingly' to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard — all three of which are inherently subjective mental states. As a textualist and originalist, I must give effect to the statutory text Congress actually enacted, not import an objective reasonableness gloss derived from Safeco Insurance Co. v. Burr, which interpreted an entirely different statute — the FCRA — with distinct text, structure, and purpose. The Seventh Circuit's application of Safeco effectively rewrites the FCA's scienter definition by substituting an objective standard for the subjective one Congress codified, which is precisely the kind of judicial legislation this Court must reject. Furthermore, Congress's explicit statement that 'no proof of specific intent to defraud is required' confirms that the scienter inquiry focuses on the defendant's actual state of mind, not whether a post hoc legal rationalization might appear objectively reasonable to a reviewing court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FCA's statutory definition of 'knowingly' under 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) expressly encompasses actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard — a three-pronged formulation that Congress deliberately crafted to focus on a defendant's subjective state of mind, not an objective reasonableness standard imported from an entirely different statute. Safeco's reasoning was grounded in the FCRA's specific use of 'willfully' and drew on common-law standards relating to physical safety, not the common law of fraud that governs the FCA context; extending Safeco wholesale to the FCA ignores this critical textual and doctrinal distinction. Just as this Court declined in Halo Electronics v. Pulse Electronics, 579 U.S. 93 (2016), to extend Safeco's objective reasonableness framework to patent willfulness because the underlying statutory text and common-law backdrop differed, the same restraint is warranted here — defendants who subjectively believed their claims were false cannot escape FCA liability merely by constructing a post-hoc objectively reasonable legal interpretation. The practical consequence of the Seventh Circuit's approach is to gut the FCA's primary anti-fraud enforcement mechanism by rewarding sophisticated actors who knowingly exploit legal ambiguity, a result inconsistent with both the statute's text and Congress's clear intent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FCA's 'knowingly' definition under 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) was deliberately crafted by Congress in 1986 to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard — a tripartite framework explicitly designed to prevent bad-faith actors from evading liability by hiding behind narrow interpretations of scienter. Importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard, developed under the FCRA's entirely distinct 'willfully' requirement, effectively nullifies two-thirds of Congress's carefully constructed definition and creates a perverse incentive for defendants to retroactively construct plausible legal interpretations after the fact, shielding those who subjectively knew their claims were fraudulent. The legislative history is unambiguous: Senator Grassley and the Senate Judiciary Committee specifically amended the FCA because courts were applying standards too favorable to defendants, and the Seventh Circuit's approach resurrects precisely the evasion Congress sought to foreclose. From a practical standpoint, allowing corporations like SuperValu and Safeway to escape FCA liability by pointing to post-hoc 'objectively reasonable' interpretations of ambiguous regulations would devastate the government's primary anti-fraud enforcement mechanism and leave vulnerable populations — including Medicaid beneficiaries overcharged for prescription drugs — without meaningful recourse.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The statutory text of 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) is dispositive here: Congress in 1986 explicitly defined 'knowingly' to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard — a carefully crafted, subjective-facing tripartite definition that leaves no textual foothold for importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard, which was constructed for the materially different 'willfully' language of the Fair Credit Reporting Act. The Senate Report accompanying the 1986 amendments confirms that Congress was deliberately expanding liability to reach defendants who subjectively knew or should have known their claims were problematic, specifically rejecting the narrow 'actual literal knowledge' standard courts had previously applied — the precise opposite of what an objective safe harbor would accomplish. Allowing defendants to retroactively construct an objectively reasonable legal interpretation as a scienter shield would gut the FCA's enforcement mechanism and reward sophisticated actors who subjectively doubted their compliance but gambled on ambiguity, which is precisely the reckless disregard Congress codified. A workable, textually coherent reading of the FCA asks what the defendant actually believed at the time of submission, not whether a reasonable lawyer could later construct a plausible defense.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) is dispositive: Congress explicitly defined 'knowingly' to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard — three subjective mental states — and expressly disclaimed any requirement of 'specific intent to defraud.' This carefully enumerated statutory definition leaves no gap for courts to fill by importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard, which was crafted to interpret the materially distinct 'willfully' requirement of the FCRA, a different statute with different text and different purposes. As a textualist, I cannot endorse the Seventh Circuit's approach of grafting an extra-textual, judicially invented multi-factor test onto a statute whose scienter terms Congress deliberately and precisely defined; doing so violates the cardinal principle that Congress's authoritative statement is the statutory text itself, not judicial glosses borrowed from inapposite statutes. Furthermore, permitting defendants to escape liability by retroactively constructing objectively reasonable legal interpretations that contradict their actual subjective beliefs at the time of submission would perversely render the FCA's scienter provision narrower than if Congress had written 'specific intent to defraud' — an absurd result no faithful reading of the statute can sustain.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The statutory text of 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) explicitly defines 'knowingly' to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard, and Congress in the 1986 Amendments expressly disclaimed any requirement of 'specific intent to defraud' — a textual framework that is fundamentally subjective in orientation and cannot be overridden by importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard, which was crafted for the distinct 'willfully' language of the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Safeco's objective standard was tethered to the specific statutory context of the FCRA and should not be mechanically transplanted into the FCA, where Congress made deliberate drafting choices about scienter that focus on what a defendant actually knew or consciously disregarded, not on what a reasonable person might have believed. Allowing defendants to escape FCA liability by retroactively constructing an objectively plausible legal interpretation — even when contemporaneous evidence demonstrates subjective awareness of falsity — would create precisely the kind of unworkable safe harbor that undermines the statute's core anti-fraud purpose and would reward sophisticated actors who can lawyer their way around clear scienter evidence. As an institutionalist matter, the Court should respect Congress's considered 1986 legislative judgment about how to define scienter rather than substitute a judicially-created objective standard that seven circuits adopted without adequate grounding in the FCA's text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) is dispositive: Congress in 1986 explicitly defined 'knowingly' to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard, and critically specified that 'no proof of specific intent to defraud' is required. This carefully crafted, self-contained definition reflects a deliberate legislative choice about the mental state required for FCA liability, and as a textualist matter, importing Safeco's objective reasonableness gloss — derived from the materially distinct 'willfully' language of the FCRA — would override Congress's own definitional work with a judicial construct drawn from a different statutory scheme. The original public meaning of 'knowingly' as defined by Congress focuses on what the defendant actually knew, believed, or consciously disregarded, not on what a hypothetical reasonable actor might have believed; Safeco's objective standard is simply incompatible with this subjective framework. Furthermore, allowing defendants to escape liability by retroactively constructing an objectively reasonable legal interpretation would directly contravene the 1986 amendments' express purpose of preventing courts from permitting bad-faith actors to evade liability through deliberate ignorance, effectively reading the 'deliberate ignorance' and 'reckless disregard' prongs out of the statute entirely.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FCA's statutory text under 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) explicitly defines 'knowingly' to encompass actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard — a three-part subjective mens rea framework that Congress deliberately crafted in the 1986 amendments to strengthen anti-fraud enforcement, not to create safe harbors for bad-faith actors. Safeco's objective reasonableness standard was developed in the context of the Fair Credit Reporting Act's 'willfully' requirement, a materially distinct statutory term and context, and mechanically transplanting that framework onto the FCA's carefully defined 'knowingly' standard disregards Congress's express textual choices and undermines the statute's remedial purpose. Allowing defendants to escape liability by retroactively constructing objectively reasonable legal interpretations — even when subjective bad faith is evident — renders the deliberate ignorance and reckless disregard prongs effectively meaningless and creates precisely the kind of procedural shield that insulates fraudsters from accountability, contrary to the FCA's core function as the government's primary tool against contractor fraud. As a former public defender who understands how legal frameworks can be weaponized to protect powerful actors while harming the public, I find the Seventh Circuit's approach deeply troubling in its practical consequences for government program integrity.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of consensus, and I find the core textual argument compelling from multiple angles. Justice Barrett's textualist framing resonates with my minimalist approach: the FCA's § 3729(b)(1) contains an explicit, comprehensive definitional provision that Congress carefully crafted in 1986, and importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard would effectively add a judicially-created safe harbor that Congress never enacted — precisely the kind of judicial overreach that undermines institutional legitimacy. The strongest argument for respondents would be that Safeco provides workable, settled expectations for regulated entities navigating ambiguous legal requirements, but as Justice Kagan correctly observes, that concern is better addressed by treating objective reasonableness as evidence bearing on subjective knowledge rather than as a categorical immunity — a narrower holding that honors the statutory text while preserving some protection for genuinely good-faith actors. As Chief Justice, I would assign the opinion with instructions to write narrowly: hold that the FCA's explicit scienter definitions are subjective and that Safeco's framework does not categorically displace them, while leaving open how objective reasonableness may inform the factual inquiry into what a defendant actually knew or believed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's textualist analysis crystallizes the core issue with precision: the Seventh Circuit's approach does not merely interpret 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) but effectively rewrites it by adding a judicially created objective reasonableness safe harbor that Congress never enacted, which is precisely the kind of judicial legislation textualism exists to prevent. The strongest argument for the respondents — that Safeco provides a workable, settled framework that prevents overdeterrence of legitimate conduct — fails on its own terms because Safeco was anchored to the FCRA's specific use of 'willfully,' a materially different term with a different common law pedigree, and the Court itself grounded that decision in FCRA-specific textual signals that are simply absent from the FCA. Justice Kagan's observation that the Seventh Circuit's rule renders subjective bad faith 'irrelevant' in fraud cases is particularly damning from a statutory coherence standpoint: if a defendant possessed actual knowledge or deliberately ignored the truth of a claim's falsity — both of which Congress explicitly enumerated as sufficient scienter — no post hoc objectively reasonable interpretation can logically negate what the defendant actually knew or consciously avoided knowing. The unanimous conference position reflects not groupthink but the genuine convergence of multiple interpretive methodologies — textualism, purposivism, and common law grounding — all pointing toward the same conclusion that the FCA's plain text controls.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett have both articulated the core textualist point with precision: the FCA's 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1) contains an explicit, comprehensive definitional provision for 'knowingly' that Congress carefully crafted in 1986, and importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard from the FCRA would effectively nullify two of the three enumerated prongs — deliberate ignorance and reckless disregard — by reducing the entire inquiry to a single objective benchmark Congress never authorized. The strongest argument for the respondents would be that Safeco represents a general common-law principle about scienter under ambiguous legal obligations, not merely an FCRA-specific rule, and that defendants should not face liability when they reasonably interpreted genuinely ambiguous legal requirements. However, that argument fails under the FCA's text because the statute's own definitions speak to what the defendant actually knew or consciously avoided knowing — if a defendant possessed subjective awareness of likely falsity, no post hoc objectively reasonable interpretation can retroactively negate that documented mental state without effectively rewriting the statute. As Justice Kagan correctly notes, objective reasonableness may remain relevant as evidence bearing on what the defendant actually believed, but it cannot function as an absolute safe harbor that renders subjective bad faith 'irrelevant,' which is precisely what the Seventh Circuit's categorical rule does.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Kagan's observation that Safeco's objective standard, if imported wholesale into the FCA, would effectively nullify the 'deliberate ignorance' and 'reckless disregard' prongs that Congress deliberately enumerated in the 1986 amendments — this is precisely the kind of judicial rewriting of statutory text that undermines Congress's anti-fraud purpose. The strongest argument for respondents would be that Safeco provides a workable, settled framework that prevents overdeterrence of legitimate business conduct and protects defendants from liability based on genuinely ambiguous legal questions, but that argument fails here because the FCA's text is not ambiguous: Congress chose subjective mental states, not an objective reasonableness benchmark, and the 1986 legislative history confirms this was a deliberate expansion of liability to close loopholes. Justice Thomas's textualist framing reinforces my own pragmatic conclusion — when the text, structure, and legislative history all point in the same direction, and when the practical consequence of the opposing rule is to reward sophisticated corporate actors who manufacture post hoc legal rationales while defrauding Medicare and Medicaid, there is no sound basis for departing from the statute as written. The Seventh Circuit's categorical rule that subjective intent is irrelevant turns the FCA into a statute that protects fraudsters rather than federal programs, and I cannot endorse that outcome.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively and persuasively reinforced the core textual point I find dispositive: Congress's explicit definitional provision in § 3729(b)(1) is a carefully constructed subjective scienter framework that admits no room for an objective reasonableness overlay imported from a different statute. Justice Barrett's observation that Safeco's transplantation would effectively add a 'fourth, judicially created safe harbor that Congress never enacted' captures precisely the textualist problem — we would be legislating from the bench in the guise of statutory interpretation. Justice Thomas's point about the distinct common law pedigree of 'willfully' under the FCRA versus 'knowingly' under the FCA further confirms that Safeco's reasoning is statute-specific and cannot travel. The strongest argument for respondents — that Safeco provides workable, administrable standards that prevent overdeterrence — is real but ultimately insufficient, because workability cannot override unambiguous statutory text, and the FCA's own framework already provides defendants meaningful protection by requiring proof of actual subjective scienter rather than mere negligence.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett's textualist analysis crystallizes the core issue precisely: the Seventh Circuit's approach doesn't merely apply Safeco — it effectively legislates a fourth scienter prong that Congress never enacted, which is the exact judicial overreach textualism exists to prevent. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that Safeco provides a workable, settled framework that prevents overcriminalization of ambiguous regulatory compliance, and that courts need some objective anchor to avoid FCA liability becoming a strict liability regime — but that argument fails because Congress already addressed this concern by excluding 'specific intent to defraud' from the statute's requirements while still demanding subjective awareness. Justice Kagan's observation that objective reasonableness may remain 'relevant as evidence bearing on what the defendant actually knew' is the correct synthesis: objective reasonableness isn't categorically irrelevant, it simply cannot operate as an absolute safe harbor that overrides direct evidence of subjective knowledge. The text of § 3729(b)(1) asks what the defendant actually knew or consciously avoided knowing, and no amount of post hoc legal rationalization can transform documented subjective bad faith into protected conduct under a statute Congress designed to expand, not contract, fraud liability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan's observation that the Seventh Circuit's approach renders subjective bad faith 'irrelevant' in fraud cases is particularly compelling from an institutionalist perspective — it is not merely a policy concern but a structural incoherence that undermines the statute's internal logic. The strongest argument for the respondent's position would be that Safeco provides workable, administrable standards that prevent FCA liability from becoming a strict liability regime for regulatory ambiguity, and that concern deserves serious weight. However, as Justice Barrett correctly notes, Congress already calibrated this balance in 1986 by expressly disclaiming specific intent requirements while simultaneously defining three subjective mental states — that legislative judgment forecloses judicial importation of an objective safe harbor from a materially different statutory scheme. My institutionalist commitment to honoring Congress's deliberate textual choices, combined with the practical reality that allowing post hoc objective rationalization to override documented subjective knowledge would hollow out the FCA's enforcement mechanism, confirms my position for the Petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch have articulated the core textualist objection with precision: the FCA's § 3729(b)(1) contains an explicit, comprehensive definitional provision enumerating three subjective mental states, and importing Safeco's objective reasonableness standard would effectively add a fourth, judicially-created safe harbor that Congress never enacted. The strongest argument for respondents — that Safeco provides a workable, administrable standard that prevents FCA liability from becoming a strict liability regime for regulatory ambiguity — fails on its own terms because the FCA already addresses this concern through its scienter requirement; a defendant who genuinely lacks actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard of falsity is not liable under the statute's own text, without any need to import an exogenous objective standard.
